source_location: Paper p. 13, Part XI: Reading the model in South Africa; Statistics South Africa QLFS Q2 2026
source_text: In Q2 2026, 5.0 million South Africans aged 15-34 were unemployed and 5.6 million were employed, producing a youth unemployment rate of 47.4 percent.
social_wording: South Africa's youth unemployment rate was 47.4% in Q2 2026: 5.0 million unemployed people aged 15-34 and 5.6 million employed.
qualifier: Observed Q2 2026 labour-market statistic; South Africa; not a model input or a forecast.

source_location: Paper pp. 3 and 5, Parts I and III; research/source/unemployment-pension/model_results.json assumptions
source_text: The scenario model follows six representative lives from age 20 to 100. Potential salary is anchored to R30,000 a month at 25; the central real wage growth is 1.5 percent, the net real return is 3 percent, and retirement begins at 60.
social_wording: The model compares six employment histories from age 20 to 100 under a common earnings opportunity and stated saving, tax and return assumptions.
qualifier: Stylized deterministic scenario model; constant 2026 rand; not actuarial advice, a microsimulation or an official forecast.

source_location: Paper pp. 3 and 6-7, Parts I and IV-V; model_results.json profiles[stable]
source_text: The stable formal profile works from 20 to 59, saves 15 percent, and reaches R4.84 million in private retirement wealth at 60.
social_wording: In the model, continuous formal work and a 15% contribution rate produce R4.84m at age 60.
qualifier: Stable-formal profile; 3% net real return; retirement at 60; constant 2026 rand.

source_location: Paper pp. 3 and 6-7, Parts I and IV-V; model_results.json profiles[temporary]
source_text: The five-year youth-shock profile is unemployed from 20 to 24, then returns to formal work as its wage scar closes by 35. It reaches R3.99 million at 60, R0.85 million or 18 percent below the stable profile.
social_wording: A five-year youth shock leaves R3.99m at 60, 18% below the stable worker, despite later recovery.
qualifier: Conditional model result; 35 employment years; constant 2026 rand; not a forecast.

source_location: Paper pp. 6-7, Parts IV-V; model_results.json profiles[delayed] and profiles[interrupted]
source_text: Entry at 30 and the interrupted-career profile each have 30 employment years. The interrupted worker finishes with R3.33 million at 60 versus R3.09 million for the age-30 entrant, about R0.24 million more because contributions made in the twenties compound through the gap.
social_wording: The same 30 employment years produce R3.33m or R3.09m depending on when they occur.
qualifier: Conditional profiles under the central 3% real return; constant 2026 rand; rounded values.

source_location: Paper pp. 6-7, Parts IV-V; model_results.json profiles[informal]
source_text: The mostly informal profile works 32 years at 70 percent of the benchmark wage, saves 5 percent and reaches R0.91 million at 60, 19 percent of stable-formal wealth.
social_wording: In the model, 32 mostly informal working years produce R0.91m at 60 because earnings and pension coverage are weaker.
qualifier: Conditional profile; constant 2026 rand; not a claim that informal work is tax-free or valueless.

source_location: Paper pp. 6 and 8, Parts IV and VI; model_results.json profiles[persistent]
source_text: Persistent exclusion leaves R148,000 at 60. The private account pays about R528 a month; the modeled R2,400 top-up supplies 82 percent of total retirement cash income of about R2,928.
social_wording: Under persistent exclusion, the model produces R528 a month privately and a R2,400 top-up: 82% of retirement cash income comes from the modeled grant.
qualifier: Stylized phased top-up, not the legal SASSA means test; constant 2026 rand; survival to 100.

source_location: Paper p. 9, Part VII and Figure 3; model_results.json catchup_rates.return_0.03
source_text: At a 3 percent real return, formal entry at 30 requires saving about 24 percent of salary to match a 15 percent saver who started at 20; entry at 35 requires 33 percent, at 40 requires 51 percent and at 45 requires 86 percent.
social_wording: At a 3% real return, the catch-up saving rate rises from 24% for entry at 30 to 86% for entry at 45.
qualifier: Modeled contribution rate needed to match the age-60 wealth of a 15% saver starting at 20; wage scar closes gradually.

source_location: Paper p. 10, Part VIII and Figure 4; model_results.json cohorts.secure/excluded fiscal_flow_by_age
source_text: Immediately before retirement, the secure one-million-person cohort contributes about R114 billion a year net of common healthcare and the excluded cohort about R74 billion. At 60, the flows reverse to modeled annual costs of roughly R14 billion and R28 billion.
social_wording: For one million modeled lives, annual net fiscal flows move from +R114bn/+R74bn before retirement to -R14bn/-R28bn at 60.
qualifier: Illustrative cohort mixes; constant 2026 rand; annual taxes minus modeled grants and public healthcare; not a population forecast.

source_location: Paper p. 11, Part IX and Figure 5; model_results.json cohorts
source_text: The secure cohort's modeled lifetime net fiscal balance is R1.87 trillion and the excluded cohort's is R0.06 trillion, a R1.80 trillion gap. About R1.25 trillion is missing tax revenue and R0.56 trillion is additional old-age grant spending; public healthcare is R1.29 trillion in both cases.
social_wording: In the model, one million excluded lives leave a R1.80tn weaker lifetime fiscal balance, driven mainly by missing taxes plus higher grants.
qualifier: Illustrative one-million-person cohorts; undiscounted lifetime totals; constant 2026 rand; rounded components.

source_location: Paper p. 12, Part X; model_results.json cohorts.secure and cohorts.excluded
source_text: In the excluded cohort, 85 percent receive at least some modeled grant versus 40 percent in the secure cohort. Average monthly grant exposure is R1,509 versus R373 per cohort member.
social_wording: The excluded cohort has broader and larger modeled grant exposure: 85% versus 40%, and R1,509 versus R373 a month on average.
qualifier: Illustrative cohort mixes and analytical top-up; not legal eligibility estimates.

source_location: Paper p. 15, Notes: Scope, limitations and sources
source_text: The model is an armchair scenario, not actuarial advice, a microsimulation or an official forecast. It uses deterministic wages and returns, retirement at 60, survival to 100 and undiscounted lifetime fiscal totals, while excluding several household and behavioural channels.
social_wording: These are conditional scenarios in constant 2026 rand, not forecasts of today's young people or the future pension budget.
qualifier: Scope boundary governing every modeled result; grant and healthcare paths are analytical assumptions.

source_location: Paper p. 14, Part XII: What can still change the path and The sequencing rule
source_text: The paper argues that the best pension reform for an unemployed 22-year-old is earlier access to stable, productive and covered work; employment should be restored before extraordinary saving is demanded, and the first contribution years should be protected.
social_wording: For an unemployed 22-year-old, pension repair starts with stable, covered work—not a more ambitious contribution rate on a zero wage.
qualifier: Policy interpretation from the model; not a quantified policy-impact estimate.

source_location: Paper p. 4, Part II: How unemployment compounds and The delayed balance sheet
source_text: A labour-market failure at 20 does not appear in the pension budget at 20. It first appears as missing assets and taxable earnings; the transfer bill arrives later, after retirement begins at 60.
social_wording: A labour-market failure at 20 can reappear in the pension budget roughly forty years later.
qualifier: Mechanism and timing interpretation under the model's retirement-at-60 assumption.
